subtype: Approach: mental simulation of living with the EMI [Thinking]
passage: Come and sit, and I will tell you how Samir and I bought our flat, because we nearly got it wrong. I am Nirmala, and back then I was twenty-five and sure a spreadsheet could tell me everything. Samir said, "Let's live it first." So for three months we moved the loan instalment we would owe into a separate account each month and lived on whatever was left. I remember thinking that if it felt tight now, it would feel worse later. The sums held. But we cancelled the trip to the hills we had planned, and I sulked about it. The test showed us the budget was workable, with hardly any room for travel. We signed, and ate a lot of home-cooked meals for years. I am glad we practised first.

qa.q: How long did Nirmala and Samir practise living on the smaller amount?
qa.a: They practised for three months.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling about the cancelled trip to the hills?
qa.a: Nirmala felt disappointed, and admits to sulking about it.

qa.q: What wise choice did the couple make before signing, and why did it help?
qa.a: They lived on the reduced income for three months first, which showed whether the loan was manageable before they were committed.

qa.q: How did Samir seem to see the trial?
qa.a: Samir saw it as a sensible way to check the plan by living it, as the words "Let's live it first" show.

grounding: Nirmala recalls practising with Samir on their income minus the loan instalment before committing.

subtype: Approach: discussing timing, finances and roles with the partner [Thinking]
passage: Our neighbours Siddharth and Indu sit at their balcony table most Sunday mornings with tea and a notebook, and this month I could not help overhearing. "If we start next year," Indu said, "who takes the leave, and for how long?" Siddharth counted on fingers. "My office is flexible for a few weeks. Yours is longer." They talked about rent, what would come out of the monthly spending, and who would do the night wakings. Siddharth asked, "And if we're not ready by then?" Indu said, "Then we say so and move the date." I do not know what either of them felt underneath. At one point Indu went quiet and looked at the road. But they were not guessing at what the other wanted. They were writing it down.

qa.q: Where do Siddharth and Indu usually sit to talk?
qa.a: At their balcony table on Sunday mornings, with tea and a notebook.

qa.q: What might Indu have been feeling when going quiet and looking at the road?
qa.a: Indu may have felt thoughtful or a little uncertain, though the narrator says they do not know what either felt underneath.

qa.q: What could the couple do if they find they are not ready by next year?
qa.a: They could move the date, as Indu says, and keep checking in together about leave, spending and night wakings.

qa.q: How does the narrator see the couple's approach?
qa.a: The narrator sees them treating the question as a joint plan rather than an assumption, since they talk through leave, money and night wakings and write it down.

grounding: A neighbour watches a couple talk through timing, leave, spending and who does what for a possible baby.

subtype: Approach: checking employer leave policy and planning finances [Action]
passage: HR note, benefits desk. Ira and Eshaan came in together and asked to read the company's leave policy for new parents line by line. I gave them printed copies and a quiet table. They marked the paid and unpaid parts, then worked out how many months of lower income they might face and wrote it in a small notebook. Ira said they wanted a savings buffer built over a year before they even start trying. Eshaan set up a monthly transfer on their phone while we spoke. I told them what the policy says and where the forms are kept. I did not advise on money or health, and I pointed them to the company's finance helpline if they wanted more. They left with copies, a plan and a date to look at it again in six months.

qa.q: How long did Ira and Eshaan plan to build the savings buffer before trying?
qa.a: They planned to build it over a year.

qa.q: What does the couple's careful reading suggest they feel about becoming parents?
qa.a: It suggests they feel serious and hopeful, and want to be prepared so money worries do not crowd out the early months.

qa.q: What could they do if the buffer is not ready in a year?
qa.a: They could look at the plan again and adjust the date or spending instead of rushing, since the point of the plan is to be ready.

qa.q: How might the HR officer have seen the visit?
qa.a: The HR officer likely saw two organised, calm people using the policy well, and took care to stay in role by giving no money or health advice.

grounding: Ira and Eshaan read the leave policy, estimate reduced income and build a savings buffer over a year before trying.

subtype: Approach: consulting a doctor for general preparation [Action]
passage: Clinic nurse's note. Varun and Pallavi booked a general check-up with the gynaecologist before they start trying for a baby. They arrived with a short list of questions about how to prepare. Pallavi said they had read a lot online but the forums kept contradicting each other. Varun added that relatives each swore by a different remedy, and they did not want to guess. The doctor listened, answered, and gave them written guidance, and both of them wrote down what they heard. I watched the two of them relax as the questions were answered. At the desk they asked when to come back and said they would follow what the doctor told them, not what gets passed around. I added no advice of my own.

qa.q: What did Varun say about the relatives?
qa.a: Varun said relatives each swore by a different remedy, so they did not want to guess.

qa.q: What does the couple's list of questions, and their comment on the forums, suggest they are feeling?
qa.a: It suggests they feel unsure and careful, and want reliable guidance instead of contradicting opinions.

qa.q: What could they do if relatives keep pushing their own remedies?
qa.a: They could thank the relatives kindly, say they are following the doctor's guidance, and check with the doctor if something worries them.

qa.q: How might the nurse have felt watching them relax?
qa.a: The nurse probably felt reassured that they were getting proper guidance, and careful to stay within the role by adding no advice.

grounding: Varun and Pallavi book a check-up for general preparation and choose the doctor's guidance over forums and relatives' theories.

subtype: Approach: planning childcare options with contingencies [Thinking]
passage: Jaya's leave would end in nine weeks and their budget had almost no slack, so Jeevan and Jaya sat at the table with a sheet of paper. Option one: Jeevan's parents, twenty minutes away. Option two: the crèche near the office, which had a waiting list. Option three: a nanny, which they could afford only a few days a week. "Grandparents first," said Jaya, "but what if your mother's knees act up?" "Then the crèche," said Jeevan, "and I'll put us on the list this week so a place isn't a surprise." For the nanny they agreed to ask one friend to be on call for emergencies. Beside each choice they wrote its backup. It did not remove the worry, but the paper made the worry smaller.

qa.q: What could the couple afford for the nanny option?
qa.a: Only a few days a week.

qa.q: What was Jaya worried about with the grandparents option?
qa.a: Jaya worried that Jeevan's mother's knees might act up, making it hard for the grandparents to help.

qa.q: What other approach could give them another safety net if two plans fail in one week?
qa.a: They could ask about flexible days or working from home at their offices, because that adds a fallback that does not depend on anyone falling ill.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's parents feel about being the first choice?
qa.a: They may feel trusted and glad to help, and perhaps also worried about letting the couple down if their health gets in the way.

grounding: Jeevan and Jaya list grandparents, a crèche and a nanny and write a backup for each in case one fails.

subtype: Approach: assuming grandparents will handle childcare [Pitfall]
passage: Suraj and Kishore never really asked. When the baby was due in the spring, they told each other that the grandparents would simply move into the flat for a few months, the way it had always been in the family. In April, on a call from Nagpur, Suraj's mother said her knees and the house made a long stay impossible, and Suraj's father agreed. Silence. The couple had no nanny's name, no crèche form, no leave application. That week they rang around, waited in office corridors with phones pressed to their ears, and paid an agency fee they had never budgeted for. It worked out, roughly. But nobody slept, and Kishore said quietly, "We should have asked before we assumed."

qa.q: What reason did Suraj's mother give on the call?
qa.a: She said her knees and the house made a long stay impossible.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel after the call, and what shows it?
qa.a: Kishore felt regretful and uneasy, shown by the quiet remark, "We should have asked before we assumed."

qa.q: What could the couple have done earlier?
qa.a: They could have asked the grandparents early on what help was really possible and drawn up backups such as a crèche or nanny list, so nothing rested on an assumption.

qa.q: How might Suraj's parents have felt when they had to explain?
qa.a: They may have felt guilty about letting the couple down, while still needing to be honest about their limits.

grounding: Suraj and Kishore assume the grandparents will move in, and scramble with no plan when they cannot.

subtype: Approach: postponing the discussion because it feels uncomfortable [Pitfall]
passage: Thursday night. Over dinner Kunal said, "So... are we ever having a baby?" and I nearly dropped my spoon. For two years I assumed we both meant "later". I never asked because it felt awkward, like touching something that might break. Turns out Kunal has been thinking of next year, and I have been thinking of five years from now, when the promotion has settled. We talked until the dal went cold. Kunal is worried about waiting too long and I am worried about money and time, and neither of us knew the other was carrying it. I wish we had spoken before it piled up. Relieved it's out, and a bit foolish. Going to set a time to talk properly on Sunday, with tea. - Bhupen

qa.q: What did Kunal ask over dinner?
qa.a: Kunal asked, "So... are we ever having a baby?"

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling at the end of the diary entry?
qa.a: Bhupen felt relieved that it was out in the open, and a bit foolish for waiting so long.

qa.q: What could Bhupen and Kunal do at the Sunday talk?
qa.a: They could each share their timeline and worries, listen fully, and look for a plan they both accept without rushing.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt during the two years?
qa.a: Kunal was probably carrying the worry about waiting too long alone, and may have wondered whether Bhupen felt the same.

grounding: Bhupen and Kunal each assume the other agrees, and discover different timelines after two years of avoiding the talk.

subtype: Approach: yielding to family pressure over the couple's own timeline [Pitfall]
passage: 'When are you giving us good news?' Divyansh's aunt asked at every wedding, and his mother had stopped hiding her hope. Damini and Divyansh had wanted to wait until the new job settled and the savings grew. But after a Diwali of comments they told each other the timeline was not worth the fight. By the following winter a baby was on the way. Damini was still on probation at the new job, and the savings were thin. Divyansh worked late to make up for it, and most nights the feeds, the worry and the chore list fell on Damini alone. Once, half asleep at the sink, Damini said, "I did this for them, not for us." Divyansh had no answer.

qa.q: Who asked "When are you giving us good news?" at every wedding?
qa.a: Divyansh's aunt asked it.

qa.q: What does Damini's remark at the sink suggest about how Damini feels?
qa.a: It suggests Damini feels resentful and overwhelmed, having followed the family's expectations rather than the couple's own wishes.

qa.q: What could the couple do now to ease the strain?
qa.a: They could sit down and share the night duties and chores more fairly, and kindly tell the relatives that they will decide their own plans, while asking a trusted person for support.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's mother feel if she heard the remark at the sink?
qa.a: She may feel sad and guilty, since her hope was meant kindly but added to the strain.

grounding: Damini and Divyansh give in to relatives' questions and start a baby before they are ready, and the stress falls mostly on Damini.

subtype: Approach: dividing household tasks before the baby arrives [Action]
passage: On Monday, Jamal and Leila set a phone alarm for two in the morning, a rehearsal week for the baby due in the autumn. Leila took the first feed with a doll, and Jamal warmed the pretend bottle. They had agreed beforehand that Jamal cooks the dinners, Leila does the laundry, and whoever is off duty gets a hard stop on being disturbed. By Wednesday the gaps showed. Nobody had planned breakfast for the one who was up. The recycling piled up by the door. On Thursday they stuck a note on the fridge: batch-cook on Sunday, one person handles mornings. By Saturday they were laughing about how tired they were after five nights of pretend. "Better here than at three with a real one," Jamal said.

qa.q: What did they stick on the fridge on Thursday?
qa.a: A note: batch-cook on Sunday, one person handles mornings.

qa.q: What does Jamal's remark at the end suggest about how Jamal feels about the rehearsal?
qa.a: Jamal feels glad and reassured, seeing the rehearsal as a cheap way to find problems early.

qa.q: What else could they rehearse before the baby arrives?
qa.a: They could practise a daytime routine or plan for a sick day, since a night test does not show everything.

qa.q: What would change for Leila if they had not rehearsed?
qa.a: Leila would meet the gaps for the first time at three in the morning with a real baby, likely with more arguments and less sleep.

grounding: Jamal and Leila run a rehearsal week of night duties and chores, and fix the gaps it shows before the baby comes.

subtype: Approach: reviewing the plan after the baby arrives [Revision]
passage: After the first month, Fatima stopped pretending to be fine. The plan had been simple: Fatima, on leave, would handle the nights while Bao worked days. But by the fourth week Fatima was falling asleep mid-sentence and had cried over a spilled cup of tea. Bao noticed the dark circles and the flat voice. That evening at the kitchen table in Rotterdam, Bao said, "This isn't working, is it?" Fatima nodded. They changed the plan: alternate nights, a part-time helper three afternoons a week, and a ten-minute check-in each evening to say how each of them was really doing. Fatima also mentioned the tiredness to the nurse at the baby clinic. By the second week of the new plan Fatima slept through until morning for the first time.

qa.q: What changes did Fatima and Bao make to the plan?
qa.a: They alternated nights, hired a part-time helper three afternoons a week, and added a ten-minute check-in each evening.

qa.q: What was Fatima feeling by the fourth week, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Fatima felt exhausted and close to tears, shown by falling asleep mid-sentence and crying over a spilled cup of tea.

qa.q: What could they do if alternating nights still leaves someone worn out?
qa.a: They could add more help or trim some duties, keep the evening check-ins, and talk it over with the clinic nurse.

qa.q: How might Bao have felt about the first plan?
qa.a: Bao may have felt worried and guilty for not noticing sooner, but relieved to change it.

grounding: After a month of exhausting nights, Bao and Fatima review the plan, alternate nights, hire help and keep checking in.
